implementation_notes: The idiomatic Kotlin pool is a coroutine dispatcher: Dispatchers.Default is a shared pool sized to the CPU count, Dispatchers.IO is a larger pool for blocking calls (64 by default, grown on demand), and dispatcher.limitedParallelism(n) derives a view of either with an explicit concurrency bound. Instead of submitting tasks to a pool you write suspend functions and wrap the CPU-heavy or blocking section in withContext(dispatcher), so the queueing and worker management disappear; structured concurrency (coroutineScope/async + awaitAll) replaces the join bookkeeping. Because the dispatchers are process-wide, isolation is expressed as a limited-parallelism view rather than a private pool.
pitfalls: Dispatchers.IO and Default are shared: one component that blocks unboundedly exhausts worker threads for every other component unless it isolates itself with limitedParallelism.
An exception in a child coroutine cancels its siblings and the parent scope - use supervisorScope where failures must stay independent.
On the JVM these dispatchers still run on Java threads, so per-task context belongs in the coroutine context, not in a ThreadLocal.

variants.name: Java Executors interop (fixed pool)
variants.implementation_notes: On the JVM an executor is one call away: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) (or newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor on JDK 21) wrapped with asCoroutineDispatcher() serves blocking and legacy code, and the executor can be used directly for Runnable APIs. Choose this when an existing Java component hands you an Executor or when executor policy detail is needed (bounded queue, rejection handler, thread factory) that dispatchers do not expose; wrap it as a dispatcher to keep suspend functions working, and close the dispatcher to shut the pool down.
pitfalls: An abandoned dispatcher leaks its threads: close() shuts the underlying executor down and is not optional.
Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so the backlog grows silently under overload.
A coroutine waiting for a task submitted to a saturated fixed pool deadlocks the same way a Java task would.
